AeroDASH: Asynchronous Vision-Language-Action Control for Continuous UAV Flight

Zhe Liu    Yuxuan Zheng    Jinzhe Qin    Ziqi Gao    Boyu Zhou ††thanks: †Corresponding Author.††thanks: $ˆ1$Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University, Shenzhen 518055, China (e-mail: z-liu26@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn; ziqigao@sz.tsinghua.edu.cn).††thanks: $ˆ2$Department of Mechanical and Energy Engineering, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen, China (e-mail: 12511006@mail.sustech.edu.cn; 12412111@mail.sustech.edu.cn; zhouby@sustech.edu.cn). Affiliation: Differential Robotics.
Abstract

Onboard inference latency creates a mismatch between the trajectories predicted by vision–language–action (VLA) policies and the ongoing motion of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). We present AeroDASH, an asynchronous VLA framework for continuous language-conditioned flight. A B-spline policy is initialized through supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations, providing continuous trajectory references in position and yaw. During execution, trajectory fusion removes the expired prediction prefix and connects the remaining segment to the active reference with derivative continuity while limiting trajectory deformation. To account for deviations induced by asynchronous execution, execution-aware group relative policy optimization (GRPO) further adapts the policy using trajectory-level rewards. On the UAV-Flow test set, AeroDASH achieves a success rate of 76.56%, exceeding OpenVLA-UAV and AeroDASH w/o GRPO by 38.1 and 20.1 percentage points, respectively. Execution experiments show that AeroDASH sustains motion during inference and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed fluctuations relative to asynchronous tracking of waypoint sequences. We further demonstrate language-conditioned flight with onboard inference and asynchronous trajectory execution. The code will be released upon acceptance.

I Introduction

Language-conditioned flight requires an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to ground natural language instructions in visual observations and translate them into continuous three-dimensional motion. Vision–language–action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for this task, learning to map visual observations and language commands directly to robot actions. However, continuous UAV flight imposes a stringent execution requirement that goes beyond discrete action prediction: the flight controller needs a temporally smooth reference between successive policy updates, with high-order derivative continuity across all degrees of freedom in the vehicle’s flat-output space.

Current VLA approaches for UAVs predict discrete waypoints or pose targets, leaving the system without a continuous reference between updates. Onboard inference latency further exacerbates this gap: during VLA inference, the UAV continues to move, so each delayed prediction is conditioned on a stale observation and arrives after part of its intended horizon has elapsed. Existing asynchronous execution strategies address this mismatch at the position level only, without enforcing the high-order derivative continuity that UAV flight controllers require across the flat-output space. Abrupt transitions in these derivatives produce large jerks that can destabilize the vehicle. A second gap lies in the mismatch between open-loop training and closed-loop execution. Supervised fine-tuning trains the policy to match individual predictions to expert demonstrations but does not directly evaluate the complete trajectory produced by asynchronous execution.

To overcome these challenges, we present AeroDASH (Fig. 1), an asynchronous VLA framework for UAVs that sustains continuous language-conditioned flight under onboard inference latency. To address the first gap, the VLA policy predicts control points that define a cubic B-spline over the quadrotor’s four-dimensional flat-output space, providing an analytically differentiable reference throughout each inference interval. When a delayed proposal arrives, the portion preceding the scheduled switch time is removed and the remaining segment is refitted to enforce high-order derivative continuity with the active reference. The fusion formulation enforces C2C^{2} continuity of the trajectory reference at switching boundaries while penalizing deviations from the retained prediction. To address the second gap, we introduce execution-aware post-training with group relative policy optimization (GRPO). We optimize the policy using trajectory-level rewards that measure agreement between the complete trajectories produced by asynchronous execution and expert demonstrations.

  • •

    We design an asynchronous B-spline fusion mechanism that aligns delayed predictions with execution time and enforces C2C^{2} continuity at switching boundaries while limiting trajectory deformation.

  • •

    We introduce GRPO post-training with trajectory-level rewards computed from asynchronously executed trajectories to improve agreement with expert demonstrations.

II Related Work

II-A Vision-Language-Action for Drones

General-purpose VLA frameworks learn language-conditioned robot actions from diverse embodied demonstrations [1, 2, 3, 4]. For UAVs, existing work spans long-horizon language-guided navigation and fine-grained flight control. AerialVLN [5] studies navigation toward a distant goal, whereas UAV-Flow Colosseo [6] pairs individual flight instructions with pilot demonstrations and trains VLA policies to predict UAV poses. Its Flying-on-a-Word tasks require the flight path to follow the spatial relationships specified by the instruction, making the executed path relevant in addition to the final position.

Reinforcement learning extends VLA training beyond demonstration imitation. SimpleVLA-RL [7] applies outcome-driven reinforcement learning to OpenVLA-OFT, using online trajectory sampling and exploration to improve manipulation performance and generalization. Its formulation provides feedback on the consequences of sequential actions, rather than supervising each prediction solely against demonstrated actions. In aerial navigation, EG-GRPO [8] augments online rollouts with expert data to guide exploration and improve alignment with fine-grained instructions.

These studies establish reinforcement learning as a means of improving instruction-conditioned behavior, while AeroDASH focuses on the effect of asynchronous execution on the resulting flight trajectory. The policy predicts B-spline control points and receives GRPO updates from closed-loop trajectory returns. This training objective evaluates successive predictions through their execution outcomes, complementing the temporal alignment and trajectory fusion discussed next.

II-B Asynchronous Trajectory Execution

Optimization-based trajectory generation provides a foundation for continuous UAV flight. Minimum-snap methods [9] penalize high-order derivatives of polynomial trajectories to generate smooth motion through prescribed waypoints. Richter et al. [10] develop an efficient formulation for jointly optimizing polynomial segments and allocating their durations. MINCO [11] further supports efficient trajectory optimization under geometric and dynamic constraints. These methods optimize flight trajectories from planning objectives and constraints; AeroDASH instead uses optimization to correct a trajectory predicted by a language-conditioned policy while limiting changes to its shape.

Receding-horizon planners update trajectories as the flight state evolves. B-spline-based systems exploit local support and analytic derivatives for online kinodynamic replanning [12, 13, 14, 15], while FASTER [16] maintains a committed trajectory during successive planning cycles. These mechanisms allow flight to continue during planning. For a VLA, however, a prediction is conditioned on an earlier visual observation and may arrive after part of its intended execution interval has elapsed. Maintaining an executable trajectory during inference therefore does not by itself resolve how the delayed prediction should be aligned and connected to it.

RTC and REMAC address asynchronous execution through action generation. RTC [17] guides new predictions using overlapping actions, whereas REMAC [18] learns delay-aware corrections and preserves the executed prefix during sampling. Both promote consistency between successive predictions, but neither explicitly imposes velocity and acceleration matching at the switching boundary.

AeroDASH aligns delayed B-spline predictions with execution time and refits the remaining curve to match the current reference’s position, velocity, and acceleration while limiting deformation. GRPO post-training further adapts the policy to asynchronous execution using closed-loop trajectory returns.

III Method

Figure 2 outlines AeroDASH’s training and execution pipeline. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initializes the B-spline policy from expert trajectories. Because the UAV continues moving during inference, optimization-based fusion aligns delayed proposals with execution time and connects them continuously to the active reference. GRPO then adapts the policy to accumulated closed-loop deviations using trajectory-level rewards.

III-A Preliminaries

AeroDASH uses an autoregressive OpenVLA policy [2] to generate B-spline trajectory proposals. At query time tqt_{q}, the policy receives oq=(Iq,ℓ,𝐬q)o_{q}=(I_{q},\ell,\mathbf{s}_{q}), where IqI_{q} is a forward-facing RGB image, ℓ\ell is the flight instruction, and 𝐬q=[xq,yq,zq,ψq]⊤\mathbf{s}_{q}=[x_{q},y_{q},z_{q},\psi_{q}]^{\top} contains the UAV position and yaw. Position and yaw form a set of flat outputs for the quadrotor model [19]. We parameterize trajectories in this four-dimensional output space. The policy generates 28 action tokens 𝐲q=(yq,1,…,yq,28)\mathbf{y}_{q}=(y_{q,1},\ldots,y_{q,28}) according to

πθ​(𝐲q∣oq)=∏j=128pθ​(yq,j∣oq,𝐲q,<j),\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}_{q}\mid o_{q})=\prod_{j=1}^{28}p_{\theta}\!\left(y_{q,j}\mid o_{q},\mathbf{y}_{q,<j}\right), (1)

where θ\theta denotes the policy parameters and 𝐲q,<j\mathbf{y}_{q,<j} contains the preceding action tokens. Detokenization and denormalization map these tokens to seven four-dimensional B-spline control points 𝐂q,ib=[xq,ib,yq,ib,zq,ib,ψq,ib]⊤∈ℝ4\mathbf{C}_{q,i}^{b}=[x_{q,i}^{b},y_{q,i}^{b},z_{q,i}^{b},\psi_{q,i}^{b}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}, i=1,…,7i=1,\ldots,7. Superscript bb denotes a local frame centered at the UAV position and aligned with its heading at tqt_{q}, with the vertical axis unchanged. Adding the fixed control point 𝐂q,0b=𝟎\mathbf{C}_{q,0}^{b}=\mathbf{0} yields eight controls that jointly parameterize a continuous flat-output trajectory.

Let 𝐂q,i\mathbf{C}_{q,i} denote the corresponding world-frame controls, obtained using the coordinate transformation in Sec. III-B. These controls define a clamped cubic B-spline with uniformly spaced interior knots [13, 15]:

𝝉^q​(u)=∑i=07Ni,3​(u)​𝐂q,i,u∈[0,1],\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{q}(u)=\sum_{i=0}^{7}N_{i,3}(u)\mathbf{C}_{q,i},\qquad u\in[0,1], (2)

where Ni,3N_{i,3} denotes the cubic B-spline basis function. The normalized phase uu corresponds to physical time t=tq+u​THt=t_{q}+uT_{H}, where TH>0T_{H}>0 is the proposal duration.

III-B Continuous Trajectory Generation

To learn continuous flight trajectories from demonstrations, the VLA needs supervision in its control-point output representation. We fit B-splines to expert flight segments and use the fitted control points as prediction targets. We then train the policy through SFT using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). Each demonstration segment contains M=8M=8 flat-output samples, expressed in the query-local frame defined in Sec. III-A and arranged as 𝐒qb∈ℝM×4\mathbf{S}_{q}^{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times 4}. For spline fitting, we map the sample indices to [0,1][0,1] using um=(m−1)/(M−1)u_{m}=(m-1)/(M-1). Before fitting, yaw angles are unwrapped to avoid artificial discontinuities at the angle wrap boundary. Let 𝚽¯∈ℝM×7\bar{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times 7} have entries Φ¯m,i=Ni,3​(um)\bar{\Phi}_{m,i}=N_{i,3}(u_{m}), i=1,…,7i=1,\ldots,7. With 𝐂q,0b=𝟎\mathbf{C}_{q,0}^{b}=\mathbf{0}, the seven control-point targets are obtained by least-squares fitting:

𝐂q,1:7b,∗=argmin𝐂∈ℝ7×4‖𝚽¯𝐂−𝐒qb‖F2.\mathbf{C}_{q,1:7}^{b,*}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{7\times 4}}\left\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{S}_{q}^{b}\right\|_{F}^{2}. (3)

The rows of 𝐂q,1:7b,∗\mathbf{C}_{q,1:7}^{b,*} correspond to the seven predicted control points.

The fitted control points are normalized and tokenized to form the target sequence 𝐲q∗\mathbf{y}_{q}^{*}. The action-token prediction loss is

ℒact=−128∑j=128logpθ(yq,j∗∣oq,𝐲q,<j∗).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}=-\frac{1}{28}\sum_{j=1}^{28}\log p_{\theta}\left(y_{q,j}^{*}\mid o_{q},\mathbf{y}_{q,<j}^{*}\right). (4)

At inference, the decoded controls are transformed into the world frame using the query position 𝐩q=[xq,yq,zq]⊤\mathbf{p}_{q}=[x_{q},y_{q},z_{q}]^{\top} and yaw ψq\psi_{q}:

𝐩q,iw=𝐑z​(ψq)​𝐩q,ib+𝐩q,ψq,iw=ψq,ib+ψq,i=0,…,7.\begin{aligned} \mathbf{p}_{q,i}^{w}&=\mathbf{R}_{z}(\psi_{q})\mathbf{p}_{q,i}^{b}+\mathbf{p}_{q},\\ \psi_{q,i}^{w}&=\psi_{q,i}^{b}+\psi_{q},\end{aligned}\qquad i=0,\ldots,7. (5)

Here, 𝐩q,ib\mathbf{p}_{q,i}^{b} is the position component of the local control point, and 𝐑z​(ψq)\mathbf{R}_{z}(\psi_{q}) denotes rotation about the vertical axis. The transformed controls 𝐂q,i=[(𝐩q,iw)⊤,ψq,iw]⊤\mathbf{C}_{q,i}=[(\mathbf{p}_{q,i}^{w})^{\top},\psi_{q,i}^{w}]^{\top} define the world-frame proposal in (2).

III-C Asynchronous Trajectory Fusion

SFT learns expert trajectories but does not enforce continuity between delayed predictions and the reference being tracked. Since the UAV keeps moving during inference, the returned prediction must first be aligned with the scheduled switch time. Temporal alignment alone does not resolve differences in the flat outputs and their first two physical-time derivatives at the switch. Fusion therefore adjusts the remaining prediction to match this boundary, avoiding abrupt changes in the reference sent to the controller.

A query at tqt_{q} produces 𝝉^q\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{q} at trt_{r}, after an inference delay of tr−tqt_{r}-t_{q} (Fig. 3). The UAV continues tracking the current reference 𝝉act\boldsymbol{\tau}^{\mathrm{act}} throughout inference and preparation, switching to the corrected proposal at tht_{h} only if accepted. The current reference must cover this entire interval.

tq\displaystyle t_{q} ≤tr≤th<tq+TH,\displaystyle\leq t_{r}\leq t_{h}<t_{q}+T_{H}, (6)
Δq\displaystyle\Delta_{q} =th−tq,uq=ΔqTH.\displaystyle=t_{h}-t_{q},\qquad u_{q}=\frac{\Delta_{q}}{T_{H}}.

Here, Δq\Delta_{q} includes inference and any further waiting before activation; uqu_{q} is the elapsed fraction of the prediction horizon. By tht_{h}, the part of the prediction assigned to [tq,th)[t_{q},t_{h}) has expired. We remove this part and, for uq<1u_{q}<1, keep the segment assigned to [th,tq+TH][t_{h},t_{q}+T_{H}]. In the prediction’s original time coordinate uu, the retained segment occupies [uq,1][u_{q},1].

To express the retained segment on the same [0,1][0,1] interval used by the spline representation, we introduce vv, with v=0v=0 at tht_{h} and v=1v=1 at tq+THt_{q}+T_{H}:

𝝉^q+​(v)\displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{q}^{+}(v) =𝝉^q(uq+(1−uq)v),v∈[0,1],\displaystyle=\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{q}\!\left(u_{q}+(1-u_{q})v\right),\quad v\in[0,1], (7)
Tq+\displaystyle T_{q}^{+} =(1−uq)​TH.\displaystyle=(1-u_{q})T_{H}.

Here, Tq+T_{q}^{+} is the remaining duration and t=th+v​Tq+t=t_{h}+vT_{q}^{+} is the physical time. Predictions with uq≥1u_{q}\geq 1 have expired and are discarded.

We first fit the remaining prediction with eight B-spline control points using regularized least squares. We translate all spatial controls by the same offset so that the retained curve starts at the active-reference position at tht_{h}, without changing yaw or the remaining duration. Let 𝐂q+∈ℝ8×4\mathbf{C}_{q}^{+}\in\mathbb{R}^{8\times 4} denote these reanchored controls. We then adjust them by solving a constrained least-squares problem. At the switch, the corrected trajectory must match the current reference in position, velocity, and acceleration, as well as yaw, yaw rate, and yaw acceleration. The objective keeps the corrected curve close to the fitted prediction and penalizes changes in its third position derivative and second yaw derivative to limit deformation.

The boundary conditions require derivatives with respect to physical time. For the original prediction, t=tq+u​THt=t_{q}+uT_{H} gives

dr​𝝉^qd​tr=TH−r​dr​𝝉^qd​ur,r∈{1,2}.\frac{\mathrm{d}^{r}\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{q}}{\mathrm{d}t^{r}}=T_{H}^{-r}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{r}\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{q}}{\mathrm{d}u^{r}},\qquad r\in\{1,2\}. (8)

For the refitted remaining segment, the same conversion uses its coordinate vv and duration Tq+T_{q}^{+}. The current reference and its derivatives are evaluated at tht_{h}.

For candidate controls 𝐂\mathbf{C}, let 𝐩𝐂​(s)\mathbf{p}_{\mathbf{C}}(s) and ψ𝐂​(s)\psi_{\mathbf{C}}(s) denote position and yaw at local physical time s∈[0,Tq+]s\in[0,T_{q}^{+}], measured from tht_{h}. The corrected controls satisfy:

𝐂qexec\displaystyle\mathbf{C}_{q}^{\mathrm{exec}} =arg⁡min𝐂∈ℝ8×4​ℒfit​(𝐂,𝐂q+),\displaystyle=\arg\min_{\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{8\times 4}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fit}}\!\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{C}_{q}^{+}\right), (9)
s.t.𝐩𝐂(r)​(0)\displaystyle\mathrm{s.t.}\quad\mathbf{p}_{\mathbf{C}}^{(r)}(0) =𝐩act(r)(th),r=0,1,2,\displaystyle=\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{act}}^{(r)}(t_{h}),\quad r=0,1,2,
ψ𝐂(r)​(0)\displaystyle\psi_{\mathbf{C}}^{(r)}(0) =ψact(r)(th),r=0,1,2.\displaystyle=\psi_{\mathrm{act}}^{(r)}(t_{h}),\quad r=0,1,2.

In (9), superscript (r)(r) denotes differentiation with respect to physical time. These constraints provide C2C^{2} continuity at the trajectory switch.

The boundary conditions specify how the new trajectory starts but leave freedom in the rest of the curve. We select the corrected trajectory by penalizing changes to the fitted remaining segment:

ℒfit=ℒcurve+λ​ℒderiv+ε​‖𝐂−𝐂q+‖F2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fit}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{curve}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{deriv}}+\varepsilon\|\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{C}_{q}^{+}\|_{F}^{2}. (10)

Here, λ\lambda weights the derivative correction term, and ε\varepsilon controls control-point regularization. The curve term measures weighted squared differences from the remaining prediction, with greater weight on its later portion. The derivative term penalizes changes in the third position derivative and second yaw derivative, normalized relative to the curve term. These derivatives are taken with respect to vv. The final term penalizes changes to the control points.

At this projection stage, a fitted proposal that already satisfies the boundary constraints remains unchanged because the objective penalizes only the correction. The projection enforces boundary continuity while minimizing changes to the retained trajectory. Before activation, the executor checks speed, acceleration, and yaw-rate bounds using the spline’s derivative control points. A candidate that passes these checks becomes the active reference at tht_{h}, with duration Tq+T_{q}^{+}. Rejected proposals and missed execution deadlines invoke a brake-to-hover fallback from the active-reference boundary. After braking, a stationary reference is maintained until the episode terminates.

III-D Execution-Aware GRPO

Accumulated closed-loop deviations shift subsequent observations away from the demonstration distribution used for SFT. We therefore adapt the policy to asynchronous execution using trajectory-level rewards and a GRPO-style update [20].

For each task ii, the pre-update policy πold\pi_{\mathrm{old}} generates KK stochastic rollouts. We compute group-relative advantages from rollout returns and use them in a token-level clipped objective. Pre-update log probabilities are recorded for sampled action tokens associated with the executed trajectory.

Asynchronous trajectory reward

We evaluate the complete executed trajectory against the expert demonstration using both position and orientation. Dynamic time warping aligns the two sequences to accommodate differences in execution speed. We use normalized dynamic time warping (nDTW) [21] as the trajectory-level reward, with higher values indicating closer agreement. Let 𝝆i=(ρi,1,…,ρi,Mi)\boldsymbol{\rho}_{i}=(\rho_{i,1},\ldots,\rho_{i,M_{i}}) and 𝝌i,k\boldsymbol{\chi}_{i,k} denote the corresponding feature sequences of the demonstration and rollout kk, respectively:

DTW⁡(𝝆i,𝝌i,k)\displaystyle\operatorname{DTW}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_{i},\boldsymbol{\chi}_{i,k}) =min⁡∑(m,n)∈WW∈𝒲⁡‖ρi,m−χi,k,n‖2,\displaystyle=\min_{W\in\mathcal{W}}\sum_{(m,n)\in W}\|\rho_{i,m}-\chi_{i,k,n}\|_{2}, (11)
Li\displaystyle L_{i} =∑m=2Mi‖ρi,m−ρi,m−1‖2,\displaystyle=\sum_{m=2}^{M_{i}}\|\rho_{i,m}-\rho_{i,m-1}\|_{2},
nDTW⁡(𝝆i,𝝌i,k)\displaystyle\operatorname{nDTW}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_{i},\boldsymbol{\chi}_{i,k}) =exp⁡(−DTW⁡(𝝆i,𝝌i,k)Li),\displaystyle=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\operatorname{DTW}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_{i},\boldsymbol{\chi}_{i,k})}{L_{i}}\right),

Here, 𝒲\mathcal{W} contains sequence alignments that preserve temporal order, and LiL_{i} normalizes the discrepancy by the demonstration’s path length in the same feature space. At the end of rollout kk, we assign Ri,k=nDTW⁡(𝝆i,𝝌i,k)R_{i,k}=\operatorname{nDTW}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_{i},\boldsymbol{\chi}_{i,k}).

Group-normalized advantages

We screen rollout groups to avoid policy-gradient updates based solely on failed or non-improving exploration. A group is retained only when at least one valid rollout exceeds a reference return threshold. The validity criterion and threshold are specified with the training settings.

For each retained group, the trajectory advantage is

Ai,k=Ri,k−R¯imax⁡(σi,η),A_{i,k}=\frac{R_{i,k}-\bar{R}_{i}}{\max(\sigma_{i},\eta)}, (12)

Here, R¯i\bar{R}_{i} and σi\sigma_{i} are the mean and standard deviation of the group’s returns, and η>0\eta>0 sets a lower bound on the normalization denominator. Both positive and negative advantages are retained. Each rollout’s advantage is shared by its action tokens used in the GRPO update.

Policy optimization

The policy objective increases the probability of sampled actions with positive advantages and decreases it for those with negative advantages. For each action token, we compare its probability under the current and pre-update policies, conditioned on the same observation and preceding tokens, denoted by hi,k,q,j=(oi,k,q,𝐲i,k,q,<j)h_{i,k,q,j}=(o_{i,k,q},\mathbf{y}_{i,k,q,<j}). Both probabilities are evaluated without sampling filters and at unit temperature:

ri,k,q,j​(θ)=pθ​(yi,k,q,j∣hi,k,q,j)pold​(yi,k,q,j∣hi,k,q,j).r_{i,k,q,j}(\theta)=\frac{p_{\theta}(y_{i,k,q,j}\mid h_{i,k,q,j})}{p_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{i,k,q,j}\mid h_{i,k,q,j})}. (13)

We retain PPO-style probability-ratio clipping [22] to constrain policy updates, yielding the following GRPO-style objective:

r¯i,k,q,j​(θ)\displaystyle\bar{r}_{i,k,q,j}(\theta) =clip⁡(ri,k,q,j​(θ),1−ϵ−,1+ϵ+),\displaystyle=\operatorname{clip}\bigl(r_{i,k,q,j}(\theta),1-\epsilon_{-},1+\epsilon_{+}\bigr), (14)
ℒclip​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta) =−𝔼i,k,q,j​[min⁡(ri,k,q,j​Ai,k,r¯i,k,q,j​Ai,k)].\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{i,k,q,j}\!\left[\min\!\left(r_{i,k,q,j}A_{i,k},\bar{r}_{i,k,q,j}A_{i,k}\right)\right].

The parameters ϵ−\epsilon_{-} and ϵ+\epsilon_{+} specify the lower and upper clipping margins. The clipped policy loss is averaged over the action tokens used in each prediction, then over predictions, rollouts, and tasks. Excluded groups contribute zero to this loss.

To discourage excessive deviation from the pre-update policy, we add a Kullback–Leibler (KL) penalty against a frozen copy, πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. The penalty is evaluated on observation and token contexts collected from greedy reference rollouts, denoted by ℋref\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{ref}}:

ℒ=ℒclip+β𝔼h∼ℋref𝒟KL(pθ(⋅∣h)∥pref(⋅∣h)).\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{clip}}+\beta\mathbb{E}_{h\sim\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{ref}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h)\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid h)\right). (15)

Here, β≥0\beta\geq 0 controls the KL regularization strength. Only the policy’s LoRA adapters are updated; the backbone and reference-policy parameters remain frozen.

IV Experiments

IV-A Experimental Setup

IV-A1 Dataset and Baselines

We evaluate all methods on 273 tasks spanning ten instruction categories in the UAV-Flow simulation test set [6]. Initial conditions and language instructions are identical across methods.

We compare AeroDASH with OpenVLA-UAV [6], the UAV-adapted OpenVLA baseline introduced in UAV-Flow. We additionally evaluate a Waypoint Chunking baseline that predicts seven waypoints per query. Both this baseline and AeroDASH produce seven four-dimensional outputs per query, represented as waypoints and B-spline control points, respectively. This comparison controls the number of predicted outputs when evaluating the action representation and execution method.

OpenVLA-UAV uses its native sequential executor. The waypoint-chunk baseline, AeroDASH w/o GRPO, and AeroDASH all use asynchronous execution. The waypoint-chunk baseline tracks the predicted waypoints sequentially. AeroDASH w/o GRPO uses the supervised policy with the same B-spline representation and trajectory-fusion executor as AeroDASH, isolating the contribution of GRPO post-training.

IV-A2 Training and Implementation Details

Both the waypoint-chunk baseline and the AeroDASH B-spline policy are trained for 50,000 SFT steps. GRPO post-training is initialized from the resulting B-spline policy and uses 2,730 tasks from the UAV-Flow-Sim training set. During GRPO, only the LoRA adapters are updated; the backbone and reference policy remain frozen. Training uses six NVIDIA RTX 4090 D GPUs. We optimize the LoRA adapters with AdamW at a learning rate of 10−510^{-5}, using rank 32 and α=16\alpha=16. GRPO uses clipping parameters ϵ−=0.20\epsilon_{-}=0.20 and ϵ+=0.28\epsilon_{+}=0.28, and a KL penalty weight of 0.01. Each iteration collects eight rollouts and one greedy reference rollout per task, with an advantage normalization floor of η=0.006\eta=0.006. Rollouts use temperature-scaled sampling with top-kk and top-pp filtering.

During GRPO rollouts and navigation evaluation, each predicted trajectory covers TH=1.4T_{H}=1.4\,s. We use a fixed inference delay of 0.60.6\,s and switch trajectories 0.70.7\,s after each query. The controller receives reference updates at 1010\,Hz while inference runs asynchronously.

A rollout terminates when the policy consistently predicts negligible motion and the executed trajectory settles.

The greedy rollout return provides the reference μiref\mu_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}} for group selection. A group is retained for GRPO updates only if at least one rollout completes normally and achieves Ri,k>μiref+ηR_{i,k}>\mu_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}+\eta. Excluded groups remain in the task average with zero GRPO contribution; the KL term is computed separately as defined in (15).

IV-A3 Controlled Trajectory Execution

Figure 5 and Table 5 compare three execution strategies across 40 conditions: five path families, four geometric instances, and two nominal speeds (0.80.8 and 1.61.6\,m/s). The families comprise straight paths, circular arcs, S-bends, ascent/descent, and rounded turns.

All three strategies use shared position/velocity feedback gains and a rigid-body/motor model. Reference commands are published at 5050\,Hz, feedback runs at 100100\,Hz, and dynamics are integrated at 11\,kHz. The position gain is 2, with velocity proportional/integral gains of 6 and 1. Waypoint Chunking updates targets every 0.20.2\,s without an arrival or settling requirement; targets have zero velocity/acceleration feed-forward. The asynchronous pair uses identical proposals with a 1.41.4\,s horizon, 0.60.6\,s inference delay, and 0.70.7\,s reference activation cadence; waypoint chunks activate at the next target-update tick after becoming eligible.

In the execution comparison, AeroDASH removes the expired prediction prefix and aligns the retained segment with the active-reference position at the switch. It optimizes the retained trajectory for smoothness while maintaining C2C^{2} continuity at the switching boundary. The controller receives analytic position, velocity, and acceleration references.

Synchronous waypoint control uses the same controller and vehicle model. It holds the target during 0.60.6\,s inference, triggered by position error ≤0.05\leq 0.05\,m and speed ≤0.05\leq 0.05\,m/s. Each query generates a 0.20.2\,s lookahead displacement from the same path rule, anchored at the measured query position.

IV-A4 Onboard Deployment

The UAV carries a Jetson Orin NX with 16 GB memory, a forward-facing RGB camera, and a PX4 flight controller. Super-LIO [23] estimates the UAV state from a Livox MID-360 LiDAR and its IMU. Images are resized to 224×224224\times 224 for policy inference. Through ROS 2 and MAVROS, the system supplies odometry and continuous trajectory references to PX4 at 5050\,Hz, independently of policy inference.

The onboard policy directly predicts B-spline control points. We use TensorRT for inference and merge the LoRA adapters before model export. Activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) [24] reduces the language model to 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), while the visual encoder and multimodal projector use mixed FP16/FP32 precision. The deployed policy has a mean inference latency of 672672\,ms on the Orin NX.

IV-A5 Evaluation Metrics

We report success rate (SR) and nDTW [21]. SR is the percentage of flights judged by manual review to satisfy the language instruction. We compute nDTW using the UAV-Flow evaluator for all methods, following the same feature representation and normalization used for the training reward in (11).

We compute execution metrics from vehicle-state histories generated by the dynamics simulation. Jerk is calculated by applying central differences directly to the raw acceleration samples at 11\,ms intervals. For each condition, we calculate mean speed v¯\bar{v}, speed standard deviation σv\sigma_{v}, and the 95th-percentile acceleration and jerk magnitudes a95a_{95} and j95j_{95} over [2.8,9.8)[2.8,9.8)\,s. Table 5 reports the equal-weight average of each metric across all 40 conditions.

IV-B Quantitative Comparison

Table I reports the closed-loop comparison on the UAV-Flow test set. AeroDASH achieves 76.56%76.56\% SR and 0.44950.4495 nDTW, compared with 38.46%38.46\% and 0.28830.2883 for OpenVLA-UAV, respectively. The SR improvement is 38.138.1 percentage points.

With both policies predicting seven four-dimensional outputs and using asynchronous execution, AeroDASH w/o GRPO achieves 56.41%56.41\% SR and 0.39130.3913 nDTW, compared with 48.72%48.72\% and 0.37520.3752 for the waypoint-chunk baseline. This corresponds to gains of 7.697.69 percentage points in SR and 0.01610.0161 in nDTW.

GRPO post-training further increases SR from 56.41%56.41\% to 76.56%76.56\% and nDTW from 0.39130.3913 to 0.44950.4495, yielding absolute gains of 20.120.1 percentage points and 0.05820.0582, respectively.

IV-C Qualitative Case Analysis

IV-C1 Language-Conditioned Task Behavior

In Fig. 4, AeroDASH follows the expert reference path more closely in Pass and exhibits less target-directed overshoot in Approach than AeroDASH w/o GRPO. In Land, AeroDASH achieves closer path agreement with the expert reference.

IV-C2 Real-World Flight

Figure 6 presents onboard image sequences and corresponding three-dimensional trajectory visualizations for streetlight passing and counterclockwise tree circling.

IV-D Execution-Strategy Comparison

Figure 5 compares vehicle motion under inference latency with shared controller and vehicle-model settings. Synchronous waypoint control produces stop-and-wait motion, averaging 0.1480.148\,m/s (Table 5). Asynchronous waypoint-chunk control maintains motion but exhibits larger speed fluctuations and higher acceleration and jerk peaks than AeroDASH.

For the asynchronous pair, Table 5 shows that AeroDASH reduces a95a_{95}, j95j_{95}, and σv\sigma_{v} by 89.7%89.7\%, 99.3%99.3\%, and 99.3%99.3\%, respectively, relative to Waypoint Chunking. All three metrics improve in every condition; mean speeds remain comparable at 1.2001.200 and 1.1981.198\,m/s, respectively.

V Conclusion

We presented AeroDASH, an asynchronous VLA framework for continuous language-conditioned UAV flight. Trajectory fusion aligns delayed B-spline predictions with the active reference while maintaining derivative continuity between successive updates. Execution-aware GRPO further adapts the policy to closed-loop deviations through trajectory-level feedback. UAV-Flow experiments demonstrate improved task success. In execution simulations, AeroDASH maintains continuous motion with lower acceleration and jerk than waypoint-based execution. Onboard flights further demonstrate language-conditioned control with policy inference and trajectory execution running concurrently.
